The difference between these two scores is displayed in the right-hand panel.This analysis was used to understand inclusion through the lens of how SGM are treated across countries at a higher level, though we acknowledge that future research ought to explore other determinants of inclusion54,55. Further research is required to investigate the factors that shape SGM inclusion in climate policies and adaptation planning across scales (from local to national) to understand why some plans include SGM while others do not. It is notable, for example, that the extent and depth of inclusion do not follow a clear pattern between countries of the Global North and Global South. Both NAPs coded for transformative capacity come from the Global South (Argentina and Bangladesh), indicating that level of SGM inclusion cannot be attributed solely to economic factors. This should include more granular analysis of which sub-populations (e.g., sexual versus gender minorities) are named in adaptation efforts, to assess whether inclusion is genuinely intersectional or limited to broad umbrella terms (e.g., LGBT). It is important to note that while indices like Equaldex offer useful comparisons, they rely on diverse sources (e.g., national surveys) that may privilege certain SGMs over others, such as the frequent exclusion of trans people.DiscussionBuilding on existing knowledge, our analysis not only incorporates a broader range of documentation to map SGM inclusion in developing NAPs, but also advances the field in two additional ways: (1) consulting a wider range of documentation on the development of national adaptation priorities, and (2) by investigating the quality of SGM inclusion in NAPs in the context of how they support transformative capacity for SGM, and how they claim to reduce their vulnerability and support climate justice through the process. We found 23 NAPs to include SGM which is a much larger amount compared to what others have found. The NAP Global Network, found 11% of published NAPs (n = 6, including only those officially submitted to the UNFCCC) included reference to LGBTQ+ populations56, while others have found only three signatories reference SGM in Nationally Determined Contributions57. It is unknown what terms were screened to identify inclusion or if systematic methods were used within this literature. The limited and uneven way in which gender (whether including SGM or not) is incorporated into adaptation practice more generally has further been noted by previous scientific studies25,28,58.Our findings suggest that favorable public opinion toward SGMs often precedes legal protections, underscoring the role of advocacy and liberation movements as key levers for advancing SGM inclusion in NAP processes59. There are opportunities to learn from practices of countries with favorable public perceptions of SGM, such as Cabo Verde that did include SGM in their NAP even though their legal protections of SGM lag behind social acceptance. Cabo Verde has long been acknowledged as a beacon of acceptance for SGM in the African region60, anecdotally linked to its strong gender equality movement61. Our results nonetheless highlight the key role of legal protections for SGM inclusion. These results should be interpreted with the understanding that they focus solely on national-level policy processes, which, while offering valuable initial insights, may overlook regional or local efforts. It is important to note that the last few UNFCCC COPs (e.g., Egypt and Saudi Arabia) have been in countries not only with low legal protections for SGM but further actively criminalize and persecute them in spite of ongoing advocacy against these host locations62,63,64, which may further hamper progress on SGM inclusion.Our findings further contribute to earlier work that identifies a connection between support for SGM in climate adaptation and the broader gender equality movement. Our analysis shows that when NAPs mention SGM, they almost always include women, often positioning SGM language directly after discussions on women. This reflects previous work that highlights shared vulnerabilities between women and SGM13 and shared history of rights-based activism65,66,67, especially in the context of feminist political ecology68 and disaster-risk reduction69. An intersectional approach can open conversations where SGM can also include women, and that these compounding marginalized identities can experience multiplicative impacts of climate change. There is an emerging area of literature that highlights how both women and SGM are disproportionately affected by gender-based violence during climate disasters and conflict13,70,71,72. Emphasizing the interconnections between these movements highlights why a power-aware intersectional approach is essential in climate negotiations on gender and adaptation. Efforts focused on a single identity (e.g., cisgender women over transgender women) overlooks synergies possible to uplift multiple groups because of shared underlying structures of oppression, such as misogyny and other systemic inequities73,74. Moving beyond a surface-level, binary understanding of gender and sex would be a significant step toward addressing these power imbalances.While progress is still needed, efforts to include women in NAPs have already driven transformative adaptation by addressing gender-specific needs, increasing participation, and directing targeted funding, particularly in the Global South25. In analyzing differences in inclusion between the Global North and Global South, it is important to recognize that countries in the Global South bear a disproportionate burden from climate change and, consequently, the need to plan for adaptation75,76,77,78. By extension, SGM communities in these countries face an additional disproportionate risk of maladaptation when adaptation planning insufficiently addresses their needs, as observed in some NAPs from Global South countries that were only partially SGM-sensitive or responsive. It is possible that even if a NAP does not include SGM, a more formalized NAP and a country with more resources for climate adaptation program implementation could have a beneficial impact on SGM. However, there are many cases in which countries that have both have SGM populations who experience discrimination, violence, and disproportionate impacts of climate change, such as the United States, Australia, and Japan8,79,80,81,82. This suggests that inclusion of SGM in the NAP is, at least, a necessary first step in addressing those harms.Our results suggest that learning from political movements could strengthen the inclusion of SGM in adaptation planning, and that broadening current gender-sensitive approaches to explicitly embrace gender diversity could further advance SGM visibility and inclusion. Work by UN bodies and the NAP Global Network signals growing institutional support for SGM inclusion in adaptation planning. For example, the NAP Global Network’s 2019 supplement to the UNFCCC Technical Guidelines highlights the importance of including sexual orientation and gender identity in NAPs83, and the Global Goal on Adaptation calls for “intersectional approaches” in adaptation action84. While our results do not confirm a direct link between such guidance and inclusive NAPs, they underscore the need for further research into how institutional frameworks like these can empower SGM inclusion.In addition to signatories and the UNFCCC secretariat, civil society has played a critical role in further advancing SGM inclusion across adaptation policies. In previous COPs, there have been some, though limited, events with a focus on SGM and intersectionality from countries, such as Canada and non-profits, such as OUT for Sustainability (OUT4S) and SustainUS85,86. The Women Environment and Development Organization (WEDO), as the focal point of the Women’s and Gender Constituency (WGC), has been an advocate of both women and SGM inclusion in the UNFCCC processes85. Likewise, the Gender and Environmental Data Alliance (GEDA)87 and the Sexual and Reproductive Health Right (SRHR) & Climate Justice Coalition88 have made important strides to increase awareness of this topic. However, these advancements follow an observed trend of exclusion of SGM advocacy groups in various intergovernmental processes relating to governance mechanisms for addressing the climate crisis59.Several practical policy recommendations can be made at the national and international level to bolster the position of SGM in climate adaptation planning. At the national level, these include89:
                
                  1.
                  
                    Including and ensuring direct participation of SGM and recognized representative organizations in adaptation planning.
                  
                
                
                  2.
                  
                    Collecting disaggregated, intersectional sexual orientation and gender identity data to us as indicators in vulnerability assessments, such as those proposed by the World Bank.
                  
                
                
                  3.
                  
                    Targeting and engaging SGM communities in educational and risk awareness campaigns on climate impacts.
                  
                
                
                  4.
                  
                    Working with recognized organizations and community centers to develop adaptation-specific capacity.
                  
                
                
                  5.
                  
                    Establishing grants prioritizing SGM and other marginalized groups, incorporating intersectional criteria and aligning with international equity standards and feminist climate adaptation literature on transformative change.
                  
                
                
                  6.
                  
                    Promoting coordinated national and international action to integrate SGM considerations into environmental policy and multilateral climate processes, leveraging partnerships, mandates, and inclusive indicators.
                  
                
              At the international level, and in preparation for future COPs, our findings highlight the need to explicitly include SGM and intersectionality in gender and climate policy discussions, particularly regarding adaptation planning, climate finance, and loss and damage. For example, institutional efforts like the Lima Work Program on Gender and the Women’s and Gender Constituency could extend outreach to SGM groups, include them in decision texts, and codify their representation. We suggest that strengthening institutional support for the intersectional inclusion of SGMs could advance the Global Goal on Adaptation by reinforcing commitments to gender-responsive, inclusive NAPs and enabling the use of equity-focused indicators to track adaptation progress. We further argue that COP negotiations, which has a strong impact on how marginalized communities are considered in adaptation planning, should only be hosted by governments that uphold basic human rights, including protections for SGM and their ability to participate without fear of violence or persecution.There are further several areas of current practice that span the local to global level that provide inspiring ways forward in this area. Although there is still limited evidence directly linking the meaningful inclusion of SGM communities in adaptation planning to measurable improvements in adaptation outcomes, an emerging body of work points to the significant opportunities such inclusion can create for both communities and adaptation practice more broadly. For example, the Waria Crisis Center in Indonesia (an organization supporting trans communities in climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction) illustrates how dedicated spaces can act as critical enabling conditions. Such spaces help surface and strengthen the inherent resilience within SGM communities, particularly through social capital, and demonstrate how this resilience can be mobilized in the face of evolving climate risks90. Additional studies underscore that organizations of this kind can serve as effective partners for national and subnational governments in consultation processes when they receive adequate financial support and formal recognition of their expertise91. The number of local, community-based organizations and international NGOs serving SGM populations and engaging with climate resilience is also growing, such as The 519 in Toronto, Canada and the Parliamentarians for Global Action, offering promising entry points for SGM participation in adaptation planning practice across scales and reduction of discrimination and violence that can arise due to climate events92,93.To conclude, from a systematic mapping of the inclusion of SGM in NAPs and supporting documents globally, we found seldom reference to the special risks faced by SGM. Further, even among those countries that did recognize SGM risks, inclusion was limited, did not include an intersectional approach, and excluded SGM subpopulations. While we welcome the progress made to date, further work needs to be done to more comprehensively include SGM in NAP processes. Future action must better support exposure reduction and adaptive capacity, as well as ensuring adaptation benefits are distributed among the various communities that encompass SGM. Our statistical results suggest that efforts towards improving social perception of SGM could be a key lever towards improving inclusion within NAPs, followed by better legal protections of SGM. However, changing public perceptions and legal protections of SGM cannot be done exogenously. Our recommendations have thus been targeted towards intergovernmental processes (like the UNFCCC and IPCC processes) that have the power to shape national priorities on climate change adaptation planning. Within these processes, the unique challenges faced by SGM demand not just acknowledgment, but visibility, inclusion, and strident action to prevent their continued erasure.MethodsBetween November 2023 and November 2024, we systematically mapped NAPs or, in the absence of an official NAP, documentation related to national adaptation planning, for all 198 countries that are members of the UNFCCC. This was guided by the systematic mapping standards set by the Collaboration on Environmental Evidence22 as well as previous work adapting these and similar standards23,24. This process can be summarized as (1) setting the objectives and scope of the mapping, (2) establishing a search and screening process, and (3) coding and extracting relevant information. Throughout these steps, an equal workload was assigned to each author (i.e., the number of countries to search, screen, and code information for). These steps are outlined below.Objectives and scope of the mapping processA mapping protocol was first established between the authors to guide what kind of information would be collected. The protocol framed what kind of subject, intervention, and outcome (or SIO) guided the search process. In terms of the subject, our study focused on SGMs. In the context of our study, SGMs include but are not limited to individuals who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, asexual, transgender, non-binary, Two-Spirit, queer, and/or intersex. This choice of language was made based on terminology used in previous work with a similar focus in different fields13. Common language describing these communities was a challenge to the screening procedure, our approach to which is outlined below. The intervention then related to the documentation of adaptation planning processes on the national level. The outcome we searched for was the inclusion of SGMs within national-level adaptation planning processes, especially in relation to climate vulnerability. Following the IPCC, we understood vulnerability to mean planning for reducing exposure or sensitivity, or otherwise supporting adaptive capacity, of SGMs3.Search procedureThe search procedure describes the process of how information about national adaptation planning processes was systematically retrieved. Given that there is diverging progress regionally on national adaptation planning globally, a variety of sources had to be consulted through a layered approach. This means that we did not limit ourselves to only countries with final plans. We also included relevant and current information about preparatory work being undertaken to prepare NAPs to gain insight into how planning processes incorporate the needs of SGM.First, the UNFCCC NAP Central database was consulted both for published NAPs from “developing”94 and “developed”95 countries. For countries without an NAP, other databases were consulted. In the case of Europe, a regional database (ClimateADAPT96) exists that tracks progress for countries in the region. The most recent adaptation plans or strategies were obtained in this way.For remaining countries that did not appear in any of these sources, an Internet search was conducted in English using Google to identify any additional NAPs, or in their absence, documentation relating to their development. To keep results concise, we used the search terms of the name of the country in addition to “national adaptation plan” or “national adaptation strategy”. The first ten results were reviewed to identify reliable and current information. Reputable sources in this regard included official governmental websites or those of NGOs or similar entities acting on behalf of countries to support them in adaptation planning processes. The only sources retained in our final analysis included those from official government websites, the Green Climate Fund (Readiness Proposals prepared for NAP development), as well as reports from other United Nations bodies (e.g., UNFCCC, FAO),To cross-reference these results, or complement them if nothing was otherwise found (especially because Internet searches were only conducted in English), additional documentation was searched for in both the UNFCCC nationally determined contributions and adaptation communications databases, which has previously been used in studies to understand adaptation planning priorities97. As a final step, the Climate Change Laws of the World database was consulted to identify any documentation relating to adaptation planning processes at the national level. Where an official NAP did not exist, all documentation found through these additional searching steps was cataloged for the combined insight they provide into national adaptation planning processes and priorities (Fig. 4 below). These additional steps were also important to mitigate the bias introduced by only conducting initial internet searches in English, as documents retrieved through additional searches were often in local languages. While this approach was pragmatic given the complexities of harmonizing global efforts across scales and sectors—particularly due to differences in language and framing—it inevitably overlooks valuable progress at other levels.                 The first three search terms allowed us to understand all references to gender, sexuality, and how the specific vulnerability of any group (whether SGM or not) are included, which we found to be a robust way of identifying whether the documents included our subject. Some search words were duplicated (i.e., gender within transgender), though we nonetheless added them as a redundancy measure in the search procedure to improve reliability. For the same reason, stems of words were also used where relevant (e.g., “vulnerab” to capture all iterations of “vulnerability”). This resulted in the inclusion of documentation from 23 countries. Where documentation was not in English, they were machine translated using Google translate, and were read in their entirety to try to mitigate the risk of translation error, rather than relying on common search terms alone. This usually meant looking more closely at sections discussing vulnerability and gender, which are common themes within the documents retrieved.Coding and data extractionWe analyzed the documentation relating to the 23 countries who provided some level of inclusion of SGM in NAPs following the content analysis approach described by Schreir98. Analysis was split equally between both authors, and the results were discussed and compared to ensure agreement with the codes applied. Although the primary analysis was divided between the two authors, both were able to review and analyze the entire sample due to its relatively small size. The brevity of the information within each document further facilitated detailed cross-checking and allowed the authors to reach consensus on the coded material. The authors met several times over the course of coding and data extraction to discuss any discrepancies that occurred.We used three categories of codes that were applied in a deductive/theory driven fashion according to their definition in existing literature. This includes (1) codes on what kind of climate vulnerability is addressed in relation to SGM within the documentation following the IPCC definition (i.e., reducing exposure, reducing sensitivity, or supporting adaptive capacity), (2) what kind (if any) of social justice dimensions are supported in relation to SGMs (understood as procedural, recognition, distributive, and restorative34), and (3) whether the inclusion of SGMs in climate adaptation planning better fits the definition of being “SGM-sensitive”, “SGM-responsive”, or “SGM-transformative” following pertinent literature in this field from research25,26,27,28,29,30,31 and practice16,32,33. Coding and synthesizing the data focused on finding references to these three categories within the set of documents found to be in-scope of the study, following previous similar stock-taking approaches23,24. Because the language of SGM-sensitive, responsive, and transformative lack widely accepted definitions, additional information is provided in the table below.In terms of the final category relating to transformation, it is important that “transformation” is defined in numerous ways even within the context of climate change adaptation alone99. Our adaptation of this theory to the goals of our study was because of its roots in feminist ideology in relation to understanding the impact of different gender-based interventions particularly in the context of climate change. It was useful in our context because of its previous applicability to the subject matter we were analyzing (adaptation planning) particularly towards delineating planning instruments with more modest impacts (i.e., being SGM-sensitive), more robust impacts (i.e., SGM-transformative), as well as being able to identify those planning processes that occupy the space in between these levels (i.e., SGM-responsive). The definition of transformation we have employed therefore relates to more recent literature that highlight several key features of the concept in action, for example, its departure not only from “business as usual” or addressing underlying drivers of the undesirable change or outcomes that are the focus of an area of policy, but rather move beyond this by encouraging more profound shifts in features of systems that create vulnerability in the first place. In our case, these include more profound shifts in values and worldviews and resulting action on addressing the vulnerability of SGM in relation to climate change within national adaptation planning processes. Building on existing literature, references to transformation relate to transformative capacity, focusing on identifying efforts that have the capacity to produce transformative change according to prevailing literature and practice, rather than actual transformative outcomes100. Given the fledgling state of literature and practice in this field, the latter would be unfeasible to analyze, though should be taken up in future studies as practical experience accumulates in this field.In coding the data, every thematic passage of text that mentioned the inclusion of SGM within the included NAPs was used as our coding unit. A generic coding unit like this was necessary because of the lack of uniformity in how and where SGM were sometimes discussed in the documents, which was also often brief. Because of the brevity of the text analyzed, the use of specific qualitative data analysis software was not deemed necessary. Rather, collaborative coding was done in a spreadsheet tool (Google Sheets). While the coding unit was the individual passages of text, our unit of analysis was the individual country NAPs (or a shared reading of the supporting documentation in their absence), as this was the focus of our study. Information collected about these processes sometimes came from multiple documents when used (e.g., NDC and AC documentation together).Data synthesisThe data were mostly presented in this study in terms of descriptive statistics, i.e., differences in distribution of how different countries adaptation planning documentation was coded. To be able to further comment on values and worldviews behind SGM inclusion in adaptation planning, we conducted further statistical analysis of differences between countries that did and did not include them on the basis of different measures of acceptance of SGM from the Equaldex, as described in the main text of this paper. This statistical analysis was done through a Wilcoxon Rank Sum test using R version 4.4.1 (2024-06-14 ucrt). This test is used to examine the association between two groups (here, countries that did and did not include SGMs in their national adaptation planning based on the systematic mapping) based on non-parametric interval data101. This is our case, given that the Equaldex data has equal intervals between values, though has no true 0 value in the absolute sense.It should be noted that while Equaldex is a robust and widely applied index to understand legal and social acceptance of SGM across different countries, it must be acknowledged that it is a generalization at a high level of abstraction (i.e., national level). It is only used here to provide a general overview of the differences between the social acceptance and legal protection of SGM among the studied countries that could provide insight towards identifying levers of social change through adaptation planning.

AbstractMarine oxygen deficient and dead zones are economically and ecologically important regions with unique impacts on marine nutrient cycling and biogeochemistry. Climatic impact-drivers expected to affect oxygen deficient zones and associated nutrient cycles include changes in temperature, wind speed, and atmospheric depositions. These climatic impact-drivers will increase sea surface temperatures that reduce oxygen solubility, increase stratification and respiration, as well as induce changes in circulation that intensify upwelling and regulate the production and emission of greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. Deoxygenation will impact biogeochemical cycles of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon. Climatic changes are likely to decrease bioavailable nitrogen and enhance sedimentary phosphorus remobilization, altering water column nutrient stoichiometry. Expansion of oxygen deficient zones can also have negative socio-economic and ecological consequences. Future research should focus on experimental and mesocosm studies, examine the responses of microbial communities, improve biogeochemical and ocean circulation models, and build and expand monitoring programs.

                        IntroductionMarine oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs) in the present-day ocean are characterized by net oxygen consumption. Marine ODZs develop when community microbial oxygen (O2) demand exceeds O2 supply from physical circulation and in situ biological production processes1,2,3. These oceanic regions with [O2] of less than 20 μmol kg−1 currently account for about 8% of the entire oceanic volume4. Oceanic regions with [O2] <5 μmol kg−1 represent about 0.1% of the total oceanic volume5. In this review, hypoxic conditions are defined as water masses characterized by [O2] <60 µmol kg−1, low oxic conditions by [O2] <10 µmol kg−1, and anoxic conditions by [O2] <1 µmol kg−1, which is close to the detection limit of typical SeaBird electrochemical sensors6. These biogeochemically distinct regions have been expanding and shoaling in the past few decades, with negative biological and economic impacts4,7. Long-term studies document an O2 decline of 0.066 µmol kg−1 yr−1 at 300 m depth, a typical core depth for open-ocean ODZs, between 50°S and 50°N over a 50-year period (1960–2010)8,9. More recent estimates point towards a global ocean O2 loss of 2% (0.072 µmol kg−1 y−1) over the past 50 years10,11,12, a process known as ‘ocean deoxygenation’. A major question arises as to the biogeochemical impacts of ocean deoxygenation and expanded marine ODZs.The ocean’s major ODZs in the Eastern Tropical South and North Pacific, the Arabian Sea, and the Bay of Bengal are generally associated with old and poorly ventilated water masses overlain by high productivity surface waters1,13. Coastal ODZs often co-occur with upwelling zones. Examples of coastal upwelling zones include eastern boundary upwelling systems, such as those off the coasts of California, Chile, Peru, Namibia, and Mauritania/Senegal (Box 1). Coastal upwelling systems bring nutrient-rich waters to the surface, which enhance primary productivity in the euphotic zone as well as organic matter supply and O2 consumption in deeper waters3,14,15. ODZs may also develop seasonally in regions, such as the West Bering Sea and the Gulf of Alaska4. Other marginal (shelf) seas or (semi-) enclosed basins, such as the Gulf of Mexico, the Baltic Sea, the Black Sea, Saanich Inlet, and the Cariaco Basin, experience areas of seasonal or complete anoxia or even hydrogen sulfide (H2S) accumulation in the water column, also referred to as “dead zones”16,17,18,19,20,21,22,23,24 (Box 1).In ODZs and anoxic waters, electron donors other than O2 are used for both heterotrophic and autotrophic processes. Indeed, the extent of ODZs is often evaluated by the occurrence of anoxic processes, such as nitrogen loss by denitrification and anammox4. These processes only occur under low-O2 or anoxic conditions and convert dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) to dinitrogen gas (N2), which constitutes a quantitatively important loss of biologically available nitrogen from the ocean4,25. Sulfate can also be used as an oxidant for organic matter respiration, producing H2S; prolonged anoxic conditions have been linked to localized fish mass mortality events as a result of accumulation of highly toxic H2S gas26.While the study of ODZ distributions and their biogeochemistry has gained considerable attention from the scientific community in recent years, including the effects of recurring climate patterns (e.g., ENSO: El Niño–Southern Oscillation) as well as mesoscale and submesoscale processes27,28,29, less is known about how climate change will affect biogeochemical cycles in ODZs. Dissolved O2 in the ocean is projected to decrease with high confidence over the coming century due to climate change30. This trend is driven by a combination of several projected high-confidence climatic impact-drivers31, including an increase in marine heatwaves, a rise in mean ocean temperature, and changes in wind patterns. The effects of other high-confidence climatic impact drivers on ODZs, such as sea level rise and ocean acidification, are not considered in this review.Ocean deoxygenation can occur directly, due to reduced gas solubility as sea surface temperature (SST) increases, and indirectly, through changes in ocean density stratification and ocean circulation and mixing24,32. Ocean deoxygenation greatly alters microbial communities and biogeochemical cycles, which influence the production of greenhouse gases, such as methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O), with corresponding feedback on climate33,34,35. Yet, many unknowns remain regarding how ODZs and their nutrient cycling will respond to ongoing and future climate change.In addition, anthropogenic stressors, such as excess nutrient input, are expected to interact with climate change effects, further impacting ODZs. The development of anoxic dead zones in coastal areas is linked to eutrophication caused by high anthropogenic nutrient loading, particularly of nitrogen and phosphorus. Examples include the Mississippi basin36, Chesapeake Bay37, and the Baltic Sea38. This review evaluates the effect of climatic impact drivers (e.g., ocean temperature increase, changes in wind patterns) on the chemical forms and distribution of macronutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon) in marine ODZs. Emerging evidence reveals complex, non-linear feedbacks between O2 loss, nutrient regeneration, and microbial community shifts, which can amplify deoxygenation and greenhouse gas production. We also summarize potential linkages between ODZ expansion and socio-economic consequences and identify key research gaps and future research priorities for better understanding the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycle dynamics in ODZs and underscore the critical need for integrated, high-resolution studies to better predict the coupled physical and biogeochemical responses of ODZs to ongoing climate change. This review is building upon the efforts of the joint Group of Experts on the Scientific Aspects of Marine Environmental Protection (GESAMP) Working Group 45 (WG45), focused on “Climate Change and Greenhouse Gas Impacts on Ocean Contaminants”. The primary removal pathway for phosphorus is burial in sediments. Most phosphorus reaches the sediment in the form of settling organic matter. While some of this organic matter will be buried, most will be microbially degraded, leading to the release of dissolved phosphate (PO43-) to porewaters. In oxic sediments, phosphorus is stored as polyphosphate (Poly-P), iron oxy(hydr-)oxides (Fe-P) or organic phosphorus (Org-P). Sediment phosphorus can be released again as DIP, especially under anoxic conditions. When concentrations of DIP are elevated, calcium phosphate minerals (Ca-P-minerals, i.e., apatite) may form, leading to the permanent removal of P from the marine environment.Box 4 Silicon cycling in ODZsDissolved silicon, in the form of silicic acid (Si(OH)4), is a critical nutrient for phytoplankton and other marine organisms that form their external skeletons and internal structures from amorphous biogenic silica (bSiO2)273,274. Autotrophic silicifiers, such as diatoms, rely on Si(OH)4 and form the base of food webs while contributing to the cycling of N, P, and C275,276, and atmospheric CO2 removal through the biological carbon pump277,278. While coastal zones receive nutrients (including Si(OH)4) from rivers and submarine groundwater discharge279, pelagic bSiO2 production is primarily fueled by upwelling of Si(OH)4 originating from deep-ocean remineralized bSiO2279. Therefore, the regeneration of Si(OH)4 from bSiO2 in sinking particles and sediments is essential for supporting silicifiers in marine ecosystems. In contrast to N and P cycling, Si is not redox sensitive, and hence its cycling is only indirectly affected by O2 conditions. As such, the role of suboxic conditions on Si(OH)4 regeneration is less studied than for N and P, but with the expansion and shoaling of marine ODZs globally, there are recent efforts to examine how oxygenation impacts Si(OH)4 cycling280,281,282,283.Because seawater is generally undersaturated with Si(OH)4, the majority of surface-produced bSiO2 dissolves as it sinks through the water column276. The dissolution rate of bSiO2 depends on the degradation of the organic layer covering diatom frustules, which is accelerated by bacterial activity after diatom cell death284. The rate of bSiO2 dissolution for particles that reach the seafloor is dependent on the degree of Si(OH)4 undersaturation in the sediment porewater and the available reactive surface area of bSiO2285. Under low O2 conditions, there is some evidence that bSiO2 dissolution may increase, either through more efficient microbial activity282 or increased degradation of diatom frustules286. The flux of Si(OH)4 released from sediments can also be affected through adsorption or release by Al- and Fe-oxides, respectively282,283,284.Bioturbating organisms typically reduce bSiO2 dissolution by transporting particles to deeper sediment layers, where dissolution is inhibited by porewaters saturated with Si(OH)4287. In the coastal Peruvian upwelling region, which includes a permanent ODZ, a lack of bioturbating organisms in the ODZ increases dissolution of bSiO2 in surface sediment layers by prolonging exposure of bSiO2 to undersaturated seawater280. Some other ecosystems, such as the seasonally anoxic fjord Saanich Inlet, have decreased bSiO2 dissolution at the sediment-water interface in anoxic compared to oxygenated zones281. This is due to the absence of demersal ground fish, which would normally resuspend sediments and increase dissolution281.In summary, there is a connection between oxygenation and availability of Si(OH)4 or remineralization of bSiO2280,281,282,283,284,285,286,287,288, mostly due to both microbial and macrofauna activity affecting the exposure time of bSiO2 particles to corrosive Si(OH)4 -undersaturated seawater. The authors of these studies note that the direct effect of O2 on bSiO2 dissolution is uncertain compared to the indirect role of sediment burial or protection of diatom frustules by organic layers. Further studies on the effects of O2, microbial activity, macrofaunal behavior, sediment type, and metal oxides are required to understand the role of ODZs on the Si cycle.Silicon cycle in ODZs. The primary source of Si(OH)4 to the oceanic water column is from upwelling of deep-ocean Si(OH)4, which originates from remineralization of biogenic silica (bSiO2). Coastal zones also receive contributions from river input and groundwater discharge. In surface waters, Si(OH)4 is assimilated by siliceous phytoplankton, mostly diatoms. Biogenic silica dissolution occurs in both oxic and anoxic waters and in sediments. The activity of benthic macrofauna indirectly affects dissolution rates by changing the exposure of bSiO2 to varying levels of Si(OH)4- undersaturated seawater and/or sediment. In contrast to the N and P cycles, the Si cycle is not redox sensitive.Impacts of climate change on ocean deoxygenation and biogeochemical cyclesGlobal warming greatly impacts the physical and biogeochemical processes that drive the development of long-term hypoxia and ODZs in marine environments, including metabolic rates, stratification, ocean circulation, and winds30. Changing winds impact upwelling intensity and atmospheric deposition30. Changes in precipitation and flooding alter anthropogenic nutrient inputs, which may amplify climatic impact-drivers44,45. In turn, ocean deoxygenation, amplified by changes in O2 solubility and associated changes in redox conditions, affects community structure and biogeochemical cycles39,46,47. The impacts of climatic drivers affecting O2 and nutrient cycles in ODZs are reviewed below. Hydrocarbon oxidation has also been associated with O2 and nutrient depletion, but it is not further discussed in this review (e.g., in the Gulf of Mexico45,48).Decrease in oxygen solubility and stratificationIncreases in mean sea surface temperatures (0.6 °C between 1980 and 2020)30 and marine heatwaves reduce the solubility of O2 and hence its availability to organisms49,50. O2 solubility decreases non-linearly with increasing temperature, e.g., corresponding to a decrease of 2.5 micromoles of O2 per half a degree Celsius (at 15 °C and salinity of 35)51,52. Therefore, the greatest impacts would be expected to occur in high-latitude regions that ventilate the ocean interior. The ocean surface temperature is projected to increase further between 2018 and 2100 on average by 0.86 [0.43–1.47, likely range] °C according to the SSP1-2.6 model projection and by 2.89 [2.01 to 4.07, likely range] °C in SSP5-8.530. Overall, warming is estimated to account for about 15% of global ocean O2 loss, and more than 50% of the oxygen loss in the upper 1000 m of the ocean10,12,24,53.Warming of the surface ocean also decreases its density, thereby enhancing stratification. Greater stratification due to warmer temperatures is primarily observed at low latitudes. By decreasing mixing and ventilation of the ocean interior, increased stratification promotes ocean deoxygenation10,53,54,55. There is a consequence of stratification that needs to be considered: a decrease in nutrient supply to surface waters from the deep-sea reservoir56. A reduced supply of limiting nutrients can lower surface ocean productivity and the subsequent export of organic matter, thereby decreasing O2 demand in underlying waters. If ventilation rates remain unchanged, lowering productivity would lead to higher regional O2 concentrations57,58,59.Changes in community structure and biological respiration ratesThe increase in temperature and decrease in O2 levels are expected to alter the composition of microbial and phytoplankton communities. For instance, different O2 regimes were shown to modulate phytoplankton diversity in the coastal tropical Southeast Pacific ODZ. New production was dominated by large phytoplankton (diatoms) with low N:P ratios ( < 16:1) in the ODZ. On the other hand, smaller (pico/nano and micro) phytoplankton with intermediate N:P ratios close to Redfield or higher ( > 20:1) were prevalent in more oxygenated subsurface waters above the shelf break and offshore. Interestingly, excess phosphate liberated from the sediments under anoxic conditions did not stimulate N2 fixation60.The biochemical response of the microbial community to variations in O2 levels is intricate and difficult to predict. This complexity arises because aerobic and anaerobic microbial processes can often occur simultaneously, even in waters with low or possibly negligible O2 concentrations. In recent years, cryptic cycling of O2 and sulfur in the anoxic zone has been discovered61,62. The expression of the metabolic pathways involved in nitrogen cycling, such as nitrification, anammox, denitrification, and inorganic carbon fixation, is also linked to changes in O2 and the distribution patterns of common ODZ microbes, such as nitrifiers (Thermoproteota, (formerly Thaumarchaeota), Nitrospina, Nitrospira), anammox bacteria (Planctomycetes), and chemoautotrophic denitrifiers (e.g., the SUP05 group within the Gammaproteobacteria)63,64. For example, Thermoproteota with active nitrification and inorganic carbon fixation are predominant in low-oxic waters, while the SUP05 group of NO3--reducing sulfur oxidizers linked to active denitrification, sulfur oxidation, and inorganic carbon fixation are more prevalent in anoxic waters63. The high abundance of SUP05 bacteria involved in inorganic carbon fixation under anoxic conditions indicates that this group is likely to play an increasingly important role in global ocean carbon and nutrient cycling as ODZs expand63.Warming also greatly increases microbial metabolic activity, respiration rates, and carbon demand65,66. O2 is consumed during organic matter degradation, with the highest O2 utilization rates in the upper thermocline59,67. Two main factors influence respiration: the supply of organic matter and the rate of enzymatic metabolic processes involved. The specific effect of temperature on biological respiration processes is influenced by several factors (depth, light, nitrogen, iron, and carbon limitation) that are overall still not well understood45. Increases in respiration rates due to warming will also affect other metabolic rates and associated biogeochemical cycling, such as nutrient limitation for phytoplankton68 or O2 production69,70. Warming and higher respiration enhance NO3- regeneration and recycling in the euphotic zone, which increases primary productivity71. Higher primary production above ODZs may lead to increased export production and O2 consumption below the euphotic zone due to the degradation and respiration of organic matter, potentially expanding these ODZs. However, metabolic activity in ODZs has been shown to decrease at lower O2 concentrations and under nutrient limitation in the Eastern Tropical South Pacific72. This decrease in metabolic activity may, in part, counteract the effect of temperature3,73,74.In addition to its impact on biological respiration rates, warming has been shown to enhance the cellular Fe-use efficiencies of N2-fixing organisms, particularly under Fe-limiting conditions75,76. Iron is an essential component of the nitrogenase enzyme, which converts atmospheric nitrogen into NH4+. An increase in primary productivity by N2-fixers at the surface could lead to increased organic matter respiration at depth, potentially contributing to the expansion of ODZs.Changes in ocean circulationChanges in ocean circulation could either increase or decrease ODZ ventilation45. For instance, the largest expansion of the equatorial Pacific ODZ was associated with a strong reduction of the equatorial Pacific circulation in Earth system models77,78.Fluctuations in near-shore hypoxia or O2 depletion in ODZs are also caused by changes in oxygen and nutrient concentrations of source waters. For instance, higher nutrient levels in source waters feeding the California Current coastal upwelling further increased primary productivity and resulted in enhanced export and respiration of the organic matter produced44,79. Both a decrease in O2 (−5%) and an increase in nutrients (+0.5%), which are realistic under current climate change projections, could expand the hypoxic zone by 20–32%. Interestingly, the combined influence from these biogeochemical drivers greatly exceeded the effects of strengthening in upwelling-favorable winds (10% increase) and global warming (3% increase) alone44.Oceanic mesoscale circulation, including eddies, plays an important role in mixing heat, carbon, and nutrients. Satellite altimetry records have shown that mesoscale eddies have been increasing by 2–5% per decade in oceanic eddy-rich regions due to ongoing climate change80. Mesoscale activity is particularly enhanced in eastern boundary upwelling systems81,82,83,84,85. Eddies may inject nutrients into the euphotic zone, enhancing primary productivity, particularly in the open ocean. In contrast, models show that eddies could suppress coastal primary productivity by transporting nutrients from the nearshore environment to the open ocean, and counteracting wind-driven upwelling in eastern boundary upwelling systems86. In the Eastern Tropical South Pacific off Peru, transport of highly productive waters offshore by an anticyclonic mode water eddy and subsequent high organic matter respiration rates promoted denitrification and near complete NO3- exhaustion (i.e., high N loss) at the center of the eddy27,85,87. N2 fixation and carbon fixation rates were concurrently enhanced in the mode water eddies88. Open-ocean low-O2 zones (with [O2] as low as 2 μmol kg−1) were also found to develop within cyclonic and anticyclonic mode-water eddies during transport from the northwestern Africa coast in the Eastern Tropical North Atlantic89,90,91. In this region, enhanced nutrient supply to the euphotic zone in anticyclonic mode-water eddies was shown to greatly increase primary productivity92. Denitrification and enhanced N loss were also reported within these eddies93. Given the broad distribution of low-O2 eddies, these processes could be relevant to all eastern boundary upwelling systems94.Similarly, changes in fine-scale ocean currents could increase periodic O2 intrusions into ODZs, sustaining aerobic NOB. These intrusions allow aerobic NOB to grow and consume O2 at the ODZ boundaries. In turn, anoxia enables anaerobic bacteria to replenish NO2-, creating a cycle that maintains the anoxic environment. Thus, NOB could provide major stabilizing feedback to ODZs volume under climate change and affect greenhouse gas production (e.g., N2O)95.Changes in upwelling intensityGlobal warming is expected to increase the temperature difference between land and sea and cause stronger upwelling-favorable alongshore winds in coastal regions, particularly at high latitudes, with both meridional and seasonal shifts in upwelling strenght96,97,98,99. Change in upwelling intensity driven by global warming is projected to increase nutrient supply to sunlit surface waters, and subsequently, export organic matter resulting from enhanced primary production at the surface and O2 consumption from respiration in deeper waters45. In the North Pacific ODZ, a study observed a concomitant increase in NO3-, PO43-, and Si(OH)4 and a decrease in O2 associated with increased wind-driven circulation100, likely related to the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation101. Other possible causes for these changes include mesoscale eddies, the phase of El Niño, and seasonal changes98. In the coastal southern Benguela upwelling system, despite a projected increase in upwelling intensity, no clear long-term trend in O2 concentration is observed102. The projected increase in upwelling intensity could reduce the extent of nutrient trapping by increasing the offshore transport of particulate materials. Reduced nutrient trapping efficiency could thus, in part, counteract ODZ expansion due to changes in upwelling intensity102.Upwelling intensity is also influenced by El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a climate phenomenon characterized by the periodic warming (El Niño) and cooling (La Niña) of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. This cyclic event influences global weather patterns, leading to shifts in precipitation, temperature, and atmospheric circulation. As such, marine heatwaves are heavily linked to El Niño, which is often responsible for extreme ocean warming. ENSO is expected to become more intense and frequent with global warming103,104. ENSO affects oceanic nutrient cycling through changes in sea surface temperatures, altering the distribution of phytoplankton and zooplankton in the equatorial Pacific. During El Niño events, warmer sea surface temperatures suppress the upwelling of nutrient-rich cold waters, reducing primary productivity, respiration, and apparent O2 utilization (AOU)59,105. Denitrification rates were also reduced (up to 70% lower) during an El Niño event, with strong implications for the nitrogen budget106. La Niña is characterized by cooler sea surface temperatures, enhancing upwelling, nutrient supply, and primary productivity. Elevated primary production by phytoplankton during La Niña events supports higher zooplankton populations, thereby cascading through the entire marine ecosystem. Water column denitrification is strongly amplified during La Niña events, driven by shoaling of the upper boundary of the ODZ107. Yet, the changes in solubility and apparent O2 utilization during El Niño and La Niña overall compensate each other, weakening the magnitude of O2 variability59.Changes in atmospheric depositionAlterations in wind patterns due to global warming will also affect atmospheric deposition of nutrients, particularly in oligotrophic open-ocean regions. Atmospheric depositions of NOx and dissolved NH4+ have tripled since the industrial108. For instance, the South China Sea is subjected to particularly high anthropogenic depositions due to its proximity to densely populated areas. An increase in nutrient inputs from the atmosphere was observed in this region and was associated with greater biological production, O2 depletion, and carbon export109,110. In contrast, ocean warming, acidification, increased stratification, and associated food web changes are also expected to affect reactive nitrogen emissions from the ocean. Elevated biological process rates under a warmer climate may increase the production of ammonia (NH3) or organic nitrogen that could efflux to the atmosphere111. The release of volatile nitrogen compounds into the atmosphere can decrease the inventory of fixed nitrogen if they are deposited on land rather than returned to the ocean, lowering primary and export production. This process may consequently reduce respiration and shrink the geographical extent and thickness of ODZs.Nutrients, particularly Fe, are mainly deposited as dust in subtropical waters of the Northern Hemisphere, which are closest to desert regions112. Atmospheric inputs of iron and fixed nitrogen could, however, be transported from their region of deposition in the subtropics to the tropics113. Atmospheric depositions were also shown to support new production in upwelling regions114. Another biogeochemical model suggests that atmospheric iron inputs could support more than 25% of the net oceanic export production, with smaller contributions from N (5%), Si (0.2%), and P (0.1%)115. For instance, iron atmospheric inputs could greatly increase N2 fixation (especially in N-limited regions)116 and primary production, enhancing organic matter respiration deeper in the water column and ODZs expansion. Yet, a global ocean model indicated that the influence of atmospheric depositions on marine primary productivity was minimal. Specifically, while atmospheric depositions contributed to an increase in primary productivity, this effect was offset by net nitrogen loss due to denitrification occurring in ODZs117.Increases in precipitation, flooding, and nutrient inputs in coastal dead zones and ODZsClimate change affects marine and terrestrial processes, such as precipitation and flooding, altering anthropogenic nutrient inputs into coastal waters from rivers and coastal groundwater118,119. Nutrient inputs, from anthropogenic or natural sources, either by rivers, estuaries, and their tributaries, or from coastal groundwater discharge, can supply nutrients to nearshore marine regions, which further exacerbate eutrophication and the potential for O2 depletion, intensifying low-O2 environments24,45,120. The effects of climate change on nutrient inputs and cycling from riverine and groundwater discharges in coastal waters are further reviewed in a companion manuscript120.Positive feedback on global warming from greenhouse gas production in ODZsAtmospheric warming is further enhanced due to the liberation of greenhouse gases, such as CH4 and N2O, that are naturally produced under low-O2 or anoxic conditions in ODZs and marine dead zones121,122,123. Thus, while nutrient inputs from atmospheric deposition, riverine inputs, and coastal groundwater discharge can enhance primary production and hence potentially act to increase carbon sinks, they can also stimulate the production of the potent greenhouse gas N2O, which is enhanced by low-O2 conditions124. N2O is 270 times more potent than CO2 on a per-molecule basis and is the main ozone-depleting substance in the stratosphere125,126. Coastal upwelling systems associated with ODZs account for up to 35 % of total oceanic N2O emissions35,125,127,128, but it is uncertain how these fluxes might change in the future. The development of anoxic conditions in dead zones or in the cores of ODZs also favors the production of the greenhouse gas CH4, which predominantly occurs in shallow near-shore environments. CH4 is 27 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than CO2 on a per molecule basis125. However, while CH4 accumulates at relatively high levels in the anoxic cores of ODZs (20–105 nM)129, it is rapidly re-oxidized to CO2 in oxic waters. Consequently, total marine CH4 emissions (6–12 Tg yr−1) account only for up to ~6% of all natural emissions130. Production of these greenhouse gases, caused by lower O2 conditions in ODZs, further enhances warming, which positively impacts ocean deoxygenation (Fig. 1). Further study is needed to examine these potential feedbacks.Socio-economic impactsProjected increases in ocean deoxygenation, the areal extent of ODZs, and changes in nutrient cycling are expected to have socio-economic impacts. Yet, the socio-economic consequences of climate change on ODZs, nutrient cycles, and marine life remain speculative due to the scarcity of statistically robust studies directly linking anthropogenic climate change to negative outcomes in ODZs and dead zones. Coastal areas provide essential ecosystem services, such as recreational activities, fisheries, transport, and energy production. The expansion of marine ODZs reduces the volume of oxic shallow waters where most human interaction with the ocean occurs and where many nutritionally and economically important species thrive. Certain microorganisms and marine animals that cannot carry out photosynthesis rely on aerobic metabolism. Minor fluctuations in O2 and nutrient levels can thus greatly affect marine ecosystems, along with associated services and functions136,137,138,139. Coastal regions, characterized by reduced ventilation and increased primary productivity, are particularly susceptible to deoxygenation. This vulnerability is exacerbated by multiple stressors, such as river influences, runoff, land use changes, and anthropogenic disturbances.Changes in O2 and nutrient levels within and surrounding ODZs and dead zones also impact fisheries and the livelihoods of human communities dependent on marine resources. Fish and shellfish industries will particularly be affected as fish are the most sensitive to hypoxia, followed by crustaceans, echinoderms, annelids, and mollusks6. However, it is important to emphasize that the taxonomic level of an organism typically provides restricted insights into the physiological effects of O2. For example, a study highlights species-specific variations instead of differences at higher taxonomic levels5. Organisms that are unable to move or possess restricted mobility, such as demersal fish, will be particularly impacted, along with benthic animals. Studies show that fish growth was impaired at O2 concentrations between 188 and 141 µmol kg−1 O2, while other aspects of aerobic metabolism are affected between 125 and 63 µmol kg−1 O26. However, even higher O2 thresholds have sublethal effects on animal behavior, ecological fitness, and geographic range, especially when the interactions with other climatic impact-drivers are considered (i.e., increase in temperature)5,139,140. Apart from supporting global food security, fish and shellfish provide many other ecosystem services, including supporting nutrient recycling in several marine habitats (e.g., coral reefs)141,142. The effects of global warming on fisheries systems also call for environmental and social justice considerations, as many impoverished and indigenous coastal communities depend on subsistence fishing. Climate impacts threaten their income, food security, and cultural heritage143,144,145.Research gaps and future research prioritiesClimate change is expected to accelerate ocean deoxygenation due to a continuous increase in temperature and impacts of other climatic-impact drivers, such as an intensification of alongshore winds and atmospheric depositions45. In turn, ODZ expansion could alter nutrient availability, thereby influencing global productivity, carbon sequestration, and greenhouse gas emissions. This review highlighted that physical and biogeochemical factors driving ocean deoxygenation and nutrient cycles are interlinked in complex ways, often synergistically, making it difficult to disentangle the impacts from individual climatic change drivers and nutrients. Also, the effects of warming and deoxygenation can be non-linear, leading to increases in metabolic rates as O2 concentrations decline to a threshold, beyond which metabolic rates decrease146. Future research priorities to better understand the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling in ODZs include improved 1) experimental and mesocosm studies, 2) microbial and genomic investigations, 3) biogeochemical modeling, and 4) high spatial and temporal resolution observations.First, more experimental and mesocosm studies are needed to isolate the effects of temperature, carbon dioxide, and deoxygenation on nutrient cycling in ODZs. For instance, it is unclear how ODZ expansion will affect nutrient regeneration versus loss by denitrification and/or anammox. The impacts of low O2 on nutrient stoichiometry (N:P:Fe ratios) and consequences for phytoplankton communities also need further investigation. Mesocosm experiments simulating future climate conditions in ODZ-like environments could help better understand the responses in nutrient cycling under isolated or multiple stressor conditions, such as warming, acidification, and deoxygenation. The feedback between ocean deoxygenation and atmospheric greenhouse gas fluxes (e.g., N2O) also requires further investigation.Second, a better understanding of the responses of microbial communities and marine organisms to warming, acidification, and deoxygenation is needed2. Several areas where more focused research is necessary include 1) investigating how the structure and function of microbial communities and higher trophic levels shift with changing O2 and nutrient regimes, 2) linking microbial diversity with nitrogen transformation pathways in ODZs using metagenomics and transcriptomics, and 3) studying how the antagonistic or symbiotic interactions (i.e., cooperation or competition) between microorganisms change under deoxygenation and warming.Third, current models often lack the resolution and complexity needed to simulate the interactions between climate-driven changes (e.g., temperature, stratification) and nutrient cycling in ODZs. A better representation of microbial metabolic diversity and its impact on nutrient (e.g., nitrogen, phosphorus, silicon) cycling needs to be incorporated into Earth system models147,148. The partitioning between denitrification, anammox, and nitrification under low-O2 conditions is also not well resolved, especially under in situ pressure conditions. Additionally, resolving future changes in atmospheric circulation, terrestrial runoff, and ocean circulation patterns and mesoscale features, such as eddies, will greatly improve biogeochemical models. Meso and sub-mesoscale processes, such as eddies, greatly influence ODZ biogeochemistry27,85,86,87,149,150. Socio-ecological models should also be used to evaluate the vulnerability of coastal communities to ODZ-induced changes in nutrient dynamics. This will allow the development of early warning systems and adaptation strategies for ecosystems dependent on coastal upwelling systems associated with ODZs for fisheries.Fourth, the lack of high-resolution observations and long-term observational datasets is a major gap in understanding current and future impacts of climatic drivers on nutrient dynamics and fluxes in ODZs and detecting trends. Higher spatial and temporal resolution could be achieved by deploying autonomous sensors (e.g., floats, gliders, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs)) and establishing sustained time series stations in ODZs. For instance, interpretation of highly resolved O2 and nutrient data obtained from the Biogeochemical Argo (or BGC-Argo) program will help improve understanding of the causes of O2 depletion and associated changes in nutrient cycles in ODZ151,152,153. One recent advance is the capability to detect NO2- at high spatiotemporal resolution using BGC-Argo floats154,155. In the future, efforts should focus on developing ocean nutrient sensors, such as PO43-, that can be deployed on autonomous platforms. Satellite data could also be used to improve long-term and spatially resolved estimates of surface productivity and nutrient limitation in ODZs.In summary, future research should use interdisciplinary methods combining field observations, including both discrete and high-resolution datasets from sensors on autonomous platforms or satellites, laboratory experiments, and earth system modeling. Shifts in nutrient dynamics can alter fisheries, food security, biodiversity, and ecosystem services. Yet, many unknowns remain, for instance, the effect of ODZs or dead zones on Si cycling is still not well understood. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the drivers and patterns of deoxygenation and the effects of deoxygenation on biogeochemical processes will help better predict future ocean productivity, manage marine resources, and mitigate climate feedback.

items.title: MartinoRossi accelera sulla sostenibilità con il nuovo bilancio 2025 e il piano 2030
items.description: MartinoRossi spa, azienda cremonese specializzata in farine, ingredienti funzionali, prodotti plant-based e proteici da cereali e legumi senza glutine
items.body:
Sostenibilità

MartinoRossi accelera sulla sostenibilità con il nuovo bilancio 2025 e il piano 2030

Redazione

-

25 Luglio 2026

Un tecnico in campo verifica irrigazione e colture, simbolo di filiera controllata e sostenibilità nel settore agroalimentare.

MartinoRossi spa, azienda cremonese specializzata in farine, ingredienti funzionali, prodotti plant-based e proteici da cereali e legumi senza glutine, ha pubblicato nel 2026 il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 a Malagnino, in provincia di Cremona, per rendicontare i risultati ambientali, industriali e sociali raggiunti nell’ultimo anno e fissare nuovi obiettivi al 2030. Il documento, diffuso dall’azienda, registra la crescita delle materie prime da filiera controllata a 108.858 tonnellate (+26% sul 2024), la riduzione dei contratti in somministrazione del 68% e il rafforzamento del percorso interno certificato Great Place to Work.
MartinoRossi adotta il nuovo standard Vsme per il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025
La novità principale del Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 è l’adozione del nuovo standard volontario Vsme, Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard, ispirato ai principi degli Esrs e all’approccio della doppia materialità. Una scelta, spiega l’azienda, pensata per anticipare le evoluzioni normative europee e rendere più leggibili le informazioni rivolte a clienti, fornitori, comunità locali e altri stakeholder. Non un passaggio solo tecnico, dunque. Anche perché nel documento viene formalizzato il primo Piano di Sostenibilità 2026-2030, con obiettivi, target e indicatori su cambiamento climatico, risorse idriche, forza lavoro propria e condotta d’impresa.
“Il Bilancio di Sostenibilità rappresenta, anno dopo anno, non solo uno strumento di rendicontazione, ma anche l’espressione concreta del nostro modo di fare impresa”, ha detto Stefano Rossi, amministratore delegato di MartinoRossi. L’ad ha parlato di una gestione “responsabile, trasparente e orientata al lungo periodo”, aggiungendo che la sostenibilità per il gruppo “non rappresenta un semplice adempimento, ma un modello di gestione che orienta ogni decisione strategica”. Parole misurate, dentro una traiettoria già tracciata. E ora messa nero su bianco.
Agrifuture e Underdrip, la ricerca nei campi di Malagnino
Uno dei capitoli centrali riguarda Agrifuture, l’azienda agricola sperimentale avviata nel 2022 su 33 ettari di proprietà accanto allo stabilimento di Malagnino. È qui che agronomi e ricercatori lavorano, in collaborazione con università e clienti, su produzione agricola sostenibile, nuove varietà, ibridi più adatti ai processi aziendali, precision farming, biostimolanti e consociazione delle colture. Un laboratorio all’aperto, con parcelle osservate stagione dopo stagione. Non una vetrina, ma un campo di prova.Leggi ancheIncubo Imu, cosa cambia nel 2025: occhio alle scadenze, ecco chi paga se sei in affittoTest della grafologia, se il partner scrive così la lettera “I” scappa a gambe levate: non è la persona che credi
Tra i progetti testati in Agrifuture c’è Underdrip, tecnologia nata da un’idea del presidente Giorgio Rossi e sviluppata con l’Università degli Studi di Milano. Il sistema brevettato di subirrigazione di precisione distribuisce acqua e fertilizzanti sotto le radici, migliorando l’efficienza d’uso delle risorse e consentendo l’applicazione localizzata di biostimolanti. Secondo i dati riportati dall’azienda, rispetto ai metodi convenzionali le pratiche di agricoltura conservativa hanno evidenziato una riduzione del 50% delle emissioni di CO₂, un calo del 50-60% del consumo d’acqua e dell’inquinamento di aria e acqua, oltre a una riduzione del 90% della lisciviazione di nitrati in falda. Dal 2025, inoltre, le sperimentazioni su Underdrip sono state orientate anche all’efficienza nell’utilizzo dell’azoto, mentre l’ERSA, Ente Regionale per lo Sviluppo Agricolo, effettua campionamenti semestrali su qualità del suolo e biodiversità microbica.
Filiera controllata in crescita: oltre 108mila tonnellate di materie prime
Le pratiche sviluppate nei campi sperimentali ricadono poi sulla filiera agricola, che resta il centro del modello industriale di MartinoRossi. Nel 2025 le materie prime provenienti da filiera controllata sono salite a 108.858 tonnellate, contro le 86.466 tonnellate del 2024, con una crescita del 26%. In parallelo, gli approvvigionamenti esterni sono scesi del 18%, fermandosi a 23.542 tonnellate. È un dato che racconta una scelta precisa: più controllo diretto, meno dipendenza da canali esterni. E, di conseguenza, una tracciabilità più stretta.
A presidiare questo sistema è Campi d’Italia, business unit incaricata di coordinare oltre 700 partner agricoli su più di 16.000 ettari coltivati. L’obiettivo dichiarato è garantire materie prime di alta qualità, prive di allergeni e Ogm, attraverso controlli lungo l’intera catena del valore. Nel frattempo l’azienda ha proseguito il piano di sviluppo industriale avviato anche grazie al Pnrr, con interventi pensati per aumentare la capacità produttiva, migliorare l’efficienza dei processi e ridurre i consumi energetici. Una crescita, insomma, legata ai campi ma anche agli impianti.
Persone, occupazione e Piano 2030: più stabilità nel gruppo
Accanto a ricerca, filiera e investimenti, il bilancio dedica spazio alla dimensione interna dell’azienda. Nel 2025 l’organico di MartinoRossi è passato da 120 a 141 dipendenti, con un incremento del 17,5%, accompagnato dall’ingresso di nuove competenze e da un rafforzamento manageriale. La certificazione Great Place to Work, ottenuta con l’89% di partecipazione al sondaggio interno, ha registrato un punteggio finale superiore di 22 punti rispetto alla media nazionale. Un segnale, secondo l’azienda, del lavoro svolto su fiducia, rispetto e valorizzazione delle persone.
Il dato più concreto, però, riguarda la stabilizzazione: i contratti in somministrazione si sono ridotti del 68% rispetto al 2024. In una fase di espansione produttiva, non è un dettaglio secondario. Nella nota che accompagna il documento, MartinoRossi spiega che il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 e il nuovo Piano 2030 confermano l’impegno a integrare obiettivi ambientali, sociali e industriali nella strategia di crescita, con target misurabili per i prossimi anni. La rotta, almeno sulla carta, è tracciata: meno impatti, più filiera controllata, più stabilità per chi lavora nel gruppo.

Concluse le analisi integrative sui campioni di vegetali a foglia larga prelevati attorno all’area dell’incendio: IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene sono presenti in concentrazioni molto basse e non costituiscono contaminazione ambientale. Trascurabile la presenza di metalli pesanti.

I risultati delle analisi concluse il 23 luglio 2026 integrano i dati di quelle concluse lo scorso 17 luglio e si riferiscono agli otto campioni di vegetali a foglia larga prelevati il 13 luglio a seguito dell’incendio all’azienda Spedi a Vecchiano (Pisa).
Nello specifico, i prelievi sono stati effettuati in sette punti considerati di massima ricaduta delle polveri e in un punto di “bianco”, situato in un’area non interessata dalla ricaduta.
Esito dei rilievi e inquinanti analizzati (vedi Rapporti di prova):

Diossine, Furani e PCB: come già comunicato, in nessuno degli otto campioni si registra la presenza di contaminazione da Diossine, Furani o PCB;
IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene: le ultime analisi concluse indicano la presenza di IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene, ma in concentrazioni estremamente basse e tali da non prefigurare un fenomeno di contaminazione ambientale;
Metalli pesanti: in base alla tipologia di materiale bruciato segnalata dalle autorità competenti, si è scelta l’estensione delle indagini anche ai metalli pesanti. Da queste analisi non sono emerse concentrazioni significative, fatta eccezione per Ferro, Alluminio e, in misura minore, Manganese. Trattandosi di elementi ubiquitari (naturalmente presenti nell’ambiente), la loro presenza non è necessariamente riconducibile alla ricaduta delle polveri dell’incendio.

Prosegue ancora la ricerca degli inquinanti riportati sopra, in campioni di filtri del PM10 di alcune stazioni di monitoraggio, tra le quali quella di Pisa Passi.

items.title: Acido picrico nei vecchi laboratori: a Brescia disinnescata una possibile tragedia
items.description: A Brescia, nei laboratori dismessi dell’ex Caffaro di via Francesco Nullo, durante le operazioni di bonifica del Sito di interesse nazionale, sono sta
items.body:
Ambiente

Acido picrico nei vecchi laboratori: a Brescia disinnescata una possibile tragedia

Redazione

-

24 Luglio 2026

Operatori specializzati ispezionano un laboratorio dismesso messo in sicurezza, con area transennata e presenza di soccorritori.

A Brescia, nei laboratori dismessi dell’ex Caffaro di via Francesco Nullo, durante le operazioni di bonifica del Sito di interesse nazionale, sono stati trovati nei giorni scorsi circa cinque chilogrammi di acido picrico secco e cristallizzato, una sostanza instabile che ha imposto lo stop immediato del cantiere per evitare rischi a tecnici e residenti. Il materiale, secondo quanto riferito dal CoGePir, il Consorzio Gestione Pirotecnici, era conservato in condizioni tali da renderlo sensibile a urti, vibrazioni, attrito e variazioni di temperatura.
Ex Caffaro, cantiere fermato dopo il ritrovamento dell’acido picrico
La segnalazione è partita dall’azienda impegnata nella messa in sicurezza dell’ex Caffaro, area industriale da anni al centro di interventi ambientali complessi. Dopo l’esame delle immagini inviate dal cantiere, il direttore generale del CoGePir, Piervittorio Trebucchi, ha chiesto di sospendere le lavorazioni, allontanare il personale e avvisare subito Vigili del Fuoco e artificieri. “Non bisognava muovere nulla”, avrebbe spiegato ai tecnici, secondo la ricostruzione del Consorzio. Solo allora l’area è stata isolata.
La Prefettura di Brescia, in base alle prime valutazioni, avrebbe preso in considerazione anche l’evacuazione di una zona con un raggio di circa un chilometro e mezzo. L’intervento degli specialisti ha poi permesso di neutralizzare il materiale, rimuoverlo e trasferirlo in un luogo idoneo, dove l’acido picrico cristallizzato è stato distrutto in condizioni controllate. Nessuno è rimasto ferito. Ma il caso, chiuso senza conseguenze, ha riaperto un tema meno visibile: la presenza di vecchie sostanze chimiche dimenticate in laboratori, scuole, ospedali e magazzini di ricerca.
Che cos’è l’acido picrico e perché diventa pericoloso
L’acido picrico, nome chimico 2,4,6-trinitrofenolo, è stato usato per anni nei laboratori di istologia, nell’industria dei coloranti e, in passato, anche come antisettico. Il suo impiego si è ridotto proprio per i problemi legati alla stabilità della sostanza. Di norma viene conservato umidificato o in soluzione acquosa; il rischio cresce quando l’acqua evapora e si formano cristalli anidri, di colore giallo, capaci di reagire con violenza a urti, calore o sfregamenti.Leggi ancheSud Italia, terremoti continui: aumenta la paura tra la gente, cosa sta succedendo davveroIn occasione della Giornata mondiale dei ghiacciai, si lancia un appello per la conservazione e la mitigazione dei cambiamenti climatici.
C’è poi un secondo elemento, non meno insidioso: il contatto con i metalli. L’acido picrico può formare picrati metallici, composti più sensibili, soprattutto in presenza di vecchi tappi, utensili o contenitori non compatibili. Per questo un flacone datato, magari con tappo bloccato o cristalli visibili sul collo, non deve essere aperto né spostato. Sembra un normale recipiente da laboratorio. Eppure, in quel momento, anche una vibrazione può diventare un problema serio.
Cosa fare davanti a un contenitore sospetto
Le indicazioni diffuse dal CoGePir sono nette: davanti a un possibile contenitore di acido picrico secco non bisogna improvvisare. Il recipiente non va toccato, mosso, aperto o fotografato da vicino; occorre allontanare le persone, impedire l’accesso al locale e chiamare immediatamente i Vigili del Fuoco e le autorità competenti. “Il tentativo di svitare un tappo può bastare”, ha spiegato il Consorzio, richiamando la necessità di lasciare ogni valutazione a personale formato.
La gestione di questi ritrovamenti richiede un coordinamento tra pubblica sicurezza, Vigili del Fuoco, responsabili delle bonifiche e operatori specializzati nel trattamento di materiali esplodenti. L’acido picrico essiccato, pur avendo caratteristiche esplosive, non coincide sempre con un ordigno dotato di innesco. Proprio per questo servono procedure chiare: stabilire se mettere in sicurezza il contenitore, rimuoverlo o procedere alla neutralizzazione sul posto è una decisione tecnica, non amministrativa né affidata al buon senso del momento.
Vecchi depositi da controllare, smaltimento solo con ditte autorizzate
Il caso di Brescia non sarebbe isolato. Secondo il CoGePir, vecchi flaconi di acido picrico possono ancora trovarsi in laboratori universitari, istituti scolastici, strutture sanitarie e magazzini di enti di ricerca. Nel maggio 2026, riferisce il Consorzio, una scuola di Genova sarebbe stata evacuata dopo il ritrovamento di una piccola quantità della sostanza nel laboratorio scientifico. La prevenzione, però, non significa aprire armadi e scatoloni senza criterio: servono inventari aggiornati, verifiche affidate a personale qualificato e procedure di emergenza già condivise.
Quando l’acido picrico è ancora utilizzato, deve essere conservato in contenitori compatibili, senza parti metalliche, mantenuto umido e controllato con regolarità. Lo smaltimento non può avvenire negli scarichi, nei normali rifiuti di laboratorio o tramite trasporto autonomo: occorrono imprese autorizzate alla gestione di rifiuti pericolosi con caratteristiche esplosive, nel rispetto delle norme ambientali e di pubblica sicurezza. Secondo i dati forniti dal Consorzio, nel 2025 il CoGePir ha raccolto e gestito oltre 51 mila chilogrammi di rifiuti pirotecnici, mentre nei primi sei mesi del 2026 ne sarebbero già stati trattati più di 40 mila. Numeri che raccontano un problema concreto: un flacone dimenticato per anni, in fondo a un armadio, può trasformarsi in una minaccia per lavoratori, cittadini e ambiente.
